observation: Cloud providers offer spot instances at typically 3–10× cheaper prices than on-demand instances, but spot instances are preemptible and their availability is highly volatile, varying strongly across zones and over time; availability can change from 100% to 0% within hours. Many workloads accept this uncertainty by checkpointing or re-executing, yet deadline-sensitive applications—such as incorporating new user data into an AI recommendation model or making timely trading decisions—cannot tolerate spot preemptions and therefore rely on expensive on-demand instances, trading cost for predictability. Thus it was unclear how deadline-bound jobs could safely exploit cheap spot resources without missing their deadlines.

solution.idea: Prior approaches fail for deadline-sensitive stateful applications because each removes only one part of the problem. Spot-market analyses show prices are opaque, zone/instance-type dependent, and change abruptly; hence any scheduler that forecasts spot availability to bid or to provision spot capacity cannot provide a hard deadline. Lineage-based recomputation gives fault tolerance but no upper bound on completion under repeated preemptions. Deadline-aware autoscaling and bidding assume a finite batch/workflow whose tasks can be restarted, so they do not preserve the monotone, durable progress required by a stateful application that must keep producing updates in every scheduling window. The right separation is not spot versus on-demand, but guaranteed progress versus opportunistic progress. We make on-demand the guarantee mechanism and spot the acceleration mechanism, and we let the current, measurable durable progress of the application decide when spot is safe to use. Concretely, for every scheduling window with a deadline D and required work W, define the on-demand rate R=W/D that would meet the deadline if used alone. Maintain a protected-progress curve P(t): the amount of work that has been completed, committed, and made durable by checkpoints/lineage; uncommitted spot work does not count. Spot preemptions may erase only uncommitted work, never P(t). A fresh on-demand fleet started after an interruption needs at most a startup delay δ before becoming productive. Therefore, from time t, R units of on-demand can still complete the window by the deadline iff P(t) is at least the fallback line F(t)=W-R(D-t-δ), equivalently R(t+δ) when W=RD. The core insight is to use this line as a control invariant. While an on-demand anchor runs, spot workers may be added at will because a spot failure cannot violate the invariant. Once spot-completed progress lifts P above a conservative margin above F(t), the scheduler cancels the on-demand anchor and lets spot carry the window alone. If spot progress stalls, the controller restarts the anchor before P can fall below the line; if all spot instances are revoked earlier, the anchor is started immediately and the invariant guarantees that enough time remains. Thus no forecast, bid model, or per-zone availability model is needed: spot availability is exploited only when it has already converted into safe, durable time lead. The key trade-off is that hard safety requires paying for at least a short on-demand anchor period and for durable checkpoints; in exchange, whenever spot capacity is genuinely available at useful throughput, the bulk of the computation can run on spot without risking the deadline. We considered and rejected probabilistic bidding and Markov availability models because the empirical spot dynamics are not transparent and not stable enough to bound a deadline. We rejected pure lineage recomputation because it bounds neither the number nor the duration of lost-progress episodes. We also rejected static mixed on-demand/spot provisioning, because without a reliable model its fixed on-demand fraction either wastes money or is unsafe. The chosen design dynamically converts spot success into safety slack and falls back to on-demand exactly when the slack is consumed.
solution.implementation: The scheduler is organized around windows of a stateful dataflow application. Each window i receives the durable state checkpoint written at the end of window i-1 and all data/updates for the window. The coordinator knows the required work W_i measured in normalized on-demand instance-seconds, the deadline D_i measured from the window's release, and R_i=W_i/D_i, the on-demand capacity that just meets the deadline. It also fixes δ, the worst-case time to launch a new on-demand fleet and restore the last durable checkpoint, and a control sampling period τ. Work within a window is decomposed into ready state-transition partitions. Every partition has RDD-style lineage: when executed on any worker, the resulting state is committed only after it is durably written to the coordinator's state store. Committed partitions increase P(t); uncommitted in-flight work is absent from P(t) and is treated as lost if its worker is preempted. The coordinator maintains P(t), the total amount of committed work in the current window, and t, the elapsed time since the window release. The main invariant is: whenever no on-demand anchor is active, P(t) must remain at least the fallback line F(t)=W_i-R_i(D_i-t-δ), with a control margin to allow reactivation. The operation of a window is as follows. At window start, P=0 and F=R_iδ, so an on-demand anchor of aggregate rate R_i is provisioned. Spot workers are also acquired whenever their current price is below the equivalent on-demand price and the spot pool has available capacity; the scheduler does not predict future prices or availability. Anchor and spot workers both fetch ready partitions and execute them. A partition's commit increments P under a per-partition two-phase commit: the partition is written to durable storage, its lineage record is appended, and only then is it announced; this makes commits atomic and prevents a preempted spot worker from creating partial progress. After each commit and at each control tick τ, the coordinator computes the distance to the fallback line. It follows three rules. First, if an anchor is active and P≥F(t)+2R_iδ (a conservative hysteresis margin), the anchor is cancelled and spot becomes the sole execution engine; the extra R_iδ buffer provides time to react if spot begins to underperform. Second, if no anchor is active and P is about to fall below F(t)+R_iδ, the coordinator immediately provisions the on-demand anchor; because one δ is needed for launch, this is low enough to require immediate action, and with the sampling period the trigger is placed at F(t)+R_iδ+R_iτ. Third, if a spot revocation is observed at any time, the coordinator launches an on-demand anchor of rate R_i right away; if an anchor was already active it simply keeps running. After a spot revocation, the coordinator uses lineage to recompute only those partitions that were uncommitted on the failed workers, while the anchor continues committed work; no completed durable work is ever redone. If P is above the fallback line when spot is revoked, the launch delay δ is already budgeted in F, so the window still meets D_i. If spot capacity continues to be plentiful and keeps P comfortably above the fallback line, the anchor remains off and spot executes nearly the whole window; if spot disappears permanently, the anchor takes over and the window still completes by deadline, at a worst-case cost equal to the original all-on-demand plan. When P reaches W_i, the coordinator performs a window-boundary checkpoint, commits the new application state as the starting state for window i+1, and starts the next window only after this checkpoint is durable; in this way continuous progress across scheduling windows is monotone because no window may carry unfinished debt into the next. The parameters have concrete meanings: R_i sets the baseline obligation of the system; δ captures both cold start and checkpoint restoration latency; τ is the control loop interval, chosen small enough that R_iτ is negligible relative to δ; and the hysteresis margin chooses how much spot must prove itself before on-demand can be safely released. The implementation requires an executor that can run both on-demand and spot workers against the same partition queue, a durable state/checkpoint store, and a coordinator that tracks partitions, commits, lineage, and the P_vs_F invariant. Spot acquisitions are deliberately spread over different instance types and zones when available at equal price, because the empirical observation shows no global availability model; the guarantee does not depend on any of them being available tomorrow, only on P staying above the fallback line. The mechanism never claims a fixed cost saving or fixed spot share: cost savings are earned on the fly, from spot work that has already been committed; if spot availability is poor, the system automatically behaves like the all-on-demand baseline and remains deadline-safe.
